analysis.one_liner: Simplifies income tax to three rates, ends special breaks for capital gains and corporations, cuts taxes for working families.
analysis.headline: The bill — which would have shifted federal taxes away from wage earners and onto capital gains, dividends, and corporate tax breaks — was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, drew zero cosponsors, and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced today's multi-bracket income tax with three rates (15%, 25%, 35%), doubled the standard deduction, created a refundable credit for state and local taxes, expanded the earned income tax credit to workers without children, and repealed the alternative minimum tax. To pay for it, it would have taxed capital gains and dividends like ordinary wages at up to 35%, set a flat 35% corporate rate while eliminating oil, gas, and other corporate tax breaks, and made companies pay tax on overseas profits instead of deferring them. It was Senator Wyden's proposal; he introduced it alone and it never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Wage-earning taxpayers, especially lower- and middle-income families, gain: the standard deduction roughly doubles (to about $15,000 for single filers and double that for couples), a new refundable credit returns 10% of state and local income, sales, and property taxes, the alternative minimum tax disappears, and workers without children become eligible for the earned income credit. Renters were promised a study on whether rent could count toward the state-and-local tax credit. savers in lower brackets also face fewer rate jumps. The bill's stated purpose was to offset the federal deficit with the revenue raised from investors and corporations, so all taxpayers share in that fiscal effect [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the basic standard deduction — to $15,000 for single filers and 200% of the indexed amount for joint filers — reducing taxable income for the millions of taxpayers who do not itemize.

Creates a refundable credit equal to 10% of state and local income, sales, real, and personal property taxes, returning cash to households in high-tax states, and directs Treasury to study counting a portion of rent as property tax so renters could benefit too.
Expands the earned income credit to workers with no children and adds a supplemental earned income child credit, a direct wage boost for the lowest-earning workers.
Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax, a parallel tax system that increasingly ensnared middle-income families who did nothing but claim ordinary deductions.
Taxes capital gains and dividends at the same rates as wages, ending a preference whose largest benefits flow to the highest-income households that hold most financial assets.

Sets a flat 35% corporate rate while ending preferential treatment for oil and gas producers (percentage depletion, intangible drilling costs, enhanced oil recovery credit), taxing the foreign income of controlled foreign corporations currently, and limiting corporate aircraft deductions — shifting the corporate tax burden away from companies without special breaks.
States the goal of partially offsetting the federal deficit with the new revenue, and asks Treasury for at least $10 billion a year in health-care tax breaks to eliminate.

analysis.who_pays: Investors in stocks and other assets, who would pay the regular rates of up to 35% on capital gains and dividends instead of the lower 15% capital gains rate [S3]. Corporations that benefit from tax preferences — oil and gas producers, multinationals deferring foreign income, and small corporations that previously paid graduated rates below 35% — would owe more [S3]. Some workers would lose specific benefits: the tax-free treatment of employer group-term life insurance, cafeteria-plan benefits, employer-provided meals and lodging, moving-expense deductions, tax-free injury compensation, parsonage allowances, the foreign earned income exclusion, and the teacher classroom-expense deduction would all be repealed [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors and corporations with tax breaks

drawbacks.text: Repealing a long list of exclusions would raise taxes on ordinary employees, not just the wealthy: workers would owe tax on employer group-term life insurance, cafeteria-plan benefits, employer meals and lodging, and moving expenses, and would lose the deduction for teachers' classroom expenses and tax-free compensation for physical injuries.

The top 35% rate begins at relatively modest incomes — $70,000 for a single filer and $120,000 for a couple — so upper-middle-class wage earners would face a 35% marginal rate on much of their income even as the bill lowers rates on capital income only for lower brackets.

The entire new system would sunset after 2010, so families and businesses would face the certainty of reverting to the old code within five years — a design choice that invites uncertainty for anyone planning long-term.

A flat 35% corporate rate replaces the current graduated schedule that charges smaller rates to smaller companies, so profitable small corporations would pay more even as large corporations lose their special preferences.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance the bill was a genuine shift of the tax burden from wages toward capital income and corporate preferences, paired with real simplification and targeted help for low- and middle-income families — the AMT repeal, EITC expansion, and refundable state-tax credit are concrete gains. But the honest cost is real: it repeals valued tax-free fringe benefits and deductions used by ordinary workers, pushes a 35% rate onto upper-middle incomes, applies a flat corporate rate that raises taxes on small corporations, and would sunset entirely after five years. It was an ambitious redesign whose distribution was progressive on paper but whose transition costs fell partly on the same households it aimed to help.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Wyden introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it; it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Wyden introduced the bill on October 27, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
He gave introductory remarks on the floor twice, on October 27 and November 1, 2005.
Not a single senator joined as a cosponsor.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors and corporations that benefit from the existing tax code came out ahead: the lower rates on capital gains and dividends, the oil and gas preferences, and the ability to defer tax on foreign income all remained untouched. The Finance Committee's inaction also preserved the individual alternative minimum tax, which continued to hit middle-income families.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Investors and corporations keeping their tax breaks

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory floor remarks twice, and secured its referral to the Finance Committee; recruited no cosponsors during the life of the bill.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other senator of either party cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no partisan split — only a single Democratic sponsor and a committee that took no action.

industries.note: The bill repeals their biggest tax breaks — percentage depletion, immediate expensing of intangible drilling costs, and the enhanced oil recovery credit — raising their cost of doing business. Those preferences have long kept the effective tax rate on the industry below the statutory rate.

Capital gains and dividends would be taxed at ordinary rates up to 35% instead of preferential rates. The benefit of the preferential rates is concentrated among the wealthiest households, which hold most taxable investment income.
The bill makes the foreign income of controlled foreign corporations taxable currently under subpart F and narrows the active-financing exception, ending the deferral of tax on overseas profits.

A flat 35% rate paired with base-broadening raises taxes on companies that shelter income through preferences but could lower it for companies paying near the top rate with few breaks. Construction contractors and other users of accounting-method preferences lose their special rules.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health benefits
industries.note: The bill only requires a Treasury study of health tax expenditures worth at least $10 billion a year — most likely the employer health insurance exclusion — so the immediate effect is nil, but the study would put the industry's largest tax shelter on the record.

Treasury would be directed to report on new reporting requirements for pass-through entities aimed at reducing tax avoidance, with data shared with state revenue agencies — a compliance threat rather than an immediate tax change.
The deduction rate for corporate aircraft use would be capped at the rate at which employees are taxed for personal use, closing a widely used perk.
